content.title: About
content.content: Beet greens are the edible leafy tops of the beet plant, harvested early in the growing season. The leaves are tender, slightly bitter, and deep green. They are eaten raw, added to salads, smoothies, or lightly cooked as a vegetable.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beet greens are rich in chlorophyll, giving them a vivid green color.
In many Eastern European cuisines they are a traditional spring salad ingredient.
The greens can also be used as animal feed, but are prized for human consumption because of their nutrient density.
They are sometimes confused with mustard greens, though they have a milder flavor.

items.title: High in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K supports blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains vitamin A and carotenoids
items.content: These nutrients aid vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C provides antioxidant protection and helps iron absorption.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Beet greens supply calcium, magnesium, and iron, important for bones and blood.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to beet greens.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Beet greens contain oxalates, which in large amounts can contribute to kidney stone formation.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Choose organic or thoroughly wash the greens to reduce exposure to chemicals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use the leaves raw in salads, blend them into smoothies, roll them in wraps, or quickly sauté with garlic. Rinse well and pat dry before consumption.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store beet greens in the refrigerator in a sealed container or a bag with a small amount of moisture for up to 3–5 days. For longer storage, blanch and freeze the greens.
